en: Īśa-Upaniṣad (Īśopaniṣad or Īśāvāsyopaniṣad), Kāṇva recension, with the commentary ascribed to Śaṃkara. Oṃ tat sat. Salutations to Brahman.
The Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad: Om. That is full, this is full; from fullness, fullness arises.
When fullness is taken from fullness, only fullness remains.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace!
The mantras beginning with "īśā vāsyam" and so forth are not employed in ritual acts,
because they reveal the true nature of the Self, which is not subordinate to ritual action.

The true nature (*yāthātmya*) of the Self—consisting of purity, being untouched by evil, oneness, eternity, bodilessness, omnipresence, and so forth, as will be explained hereafter—is incompatible with ritual action (*karman*). Therefore, it is entirely appropriate that these [passages] are not applied to ritual actions.

For the true nature of the Self, characterized in this way, is not something to be produced, modified, attained, or refined; nor is it of the nature of an agent or an enjoyer, such that it could be subordinate to ritual action.
Since all the Upaniṣads reach their conclusion solely through the determination of the true nature of the Self (ātman),
and since the Gītās and the Mokṣadharma treatises likewise have this as their ultimate purpose,

therefore, rites are prescribed based on actions established by worldly cognition, taking into account the multiplicity of the self, its status as agent and enjoyer, as well as its impurity and being untouched by sin.

For those who know the rules of qualification (*adhikāra*) declare that a twice-born person who, desiring the fruit of action— both visible, such as Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*), and invisible, such as heaven— considers himself thus: "I am a twice-born man, and I do not possess qualities such as being one-eyed or hunchbacked which would render me ineligible," is indeed qualified for ritual actions.

Therefore, by revealing the true nature of the Self, these mantras remove the innate ignorance regarding the Self and generate the knowledge of the oneness of the Self and so forth, which is the means for severing the attributes of transmigratory existence such as sorrow and delusion.
Thus, we shall provide a brief commentary on these mantras, whose qualified recipient, subject matter, relationship, and purpose have been stated. Om.
All this is to be pervaded by the Lord—whatever moves in this world.
Enjoy what has been surrendered by him; do not covet anyone's wealth.
One who rules is a ruler (*iṭ*); therefore, he is *Īśā*.
He is the Ruler, the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self of all.

For he rules over everything, being the Self of all living beings by way of being their innermost self (*pratyagātman*). By that very form of his own, he is the one for whom the "to-be-covered" (*vāsya*)—that which is to be veiled—is [the object].

What is this? All this—whatever exists whatsoever in the world, on the earth—that entire universe is to be covered by its own Self, the Lord, as the innermost self (pratyagātman), with the realization "I am indeed all this," in the form of the ultimate truth; for all this, including the moving and the unmoving, is unreal and must be covered by its own Supreme Self.

Just as the adventitious foul odor of sandalwood, agallochum, and the like, produced by contact with water and resulting in moisture and so forth, is covered by rubbing away that [adventitious] nature through its own essential fragrance which is the ultimate reality.

In the very same way, the natural state of being an agent and an enjoyer—which is superimposed upon one's own self and characterized by the world—is, through the contemplation of the nature of the ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*), abandoned within the "world" (the earth); for the phrase "in the world" is intended as an illustration, meaning that the entire aggregate of transformations known as name, form, and action is abandoned.

Thus, for one who is disciplined in the contemplation of the Self as the Lord (*īśvara*), the qualification belongs solely to the renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) of the three desires, such as for a son, and not to ritual actions (*karman*).
The meaning is "by that renunciation which has been abandoned.

For a son or a servant who has been renounced—having died—is not able to protect oneself, because of the absence of any connection with the self; therefore, the meaning of the Veda is simply "by renunciation," i.e., you should enjoy, you should protect [yourself]. Thus, having renounced all desires, do not covet; do not form a longing or craving for wealth. The meaning is: do not desire the wealth of anyone whatsoever, whether it be the wealth of another or one's own.
The particle *svid* is an expletive. Alternatively, it means "do not covet.
Why? Because the phrase "whose wealth indeed? has an interrogative force implying that there is no one's wealth at all that could be coveted.

The meaning is: since everything has been renounced through the contemplation of the Lord that "the Self alone is all this," and because all this belongs to the Self alone and the Self indeed is all, you should not harbor greed for false objects.

Thus, for one who knows the Self, the Self must be protected by renouncing the threefold desire for sons and so forth, through steadfastness in the knowledge of the Self; this is the meaning of the Veda.
Now, the mantra teaches this to the other person, who—being ignorant of the Self—is incapable of grasping the Self: "Performing indeed actions here, one should desire to live a hundred years."
Thus it is with you; there is no other way than this: action does not cling to a man.

"Performing indeed" here means performing the rites such as the *agnihotra* and others; "desiring to live" means wishing to live for a hundred years—that is, for a hundred years in number, for that much is determined to be the maximum lifespan of a person.
Thus, by restating what is already established—that one desires to live for a hundred years—it is enjoined that one should do so "performing indeed the rites."

In this very manner, while you— a man conceiving the pride of being merely a human— desire to live, there is no other way than the present mode of performing rites such as the Agnihotra by which one is not smeared by inauspicious action; the meaning is that one is not tainted by action.
Therefore, one who desires to live should indeed perform the rites prescribed by the scriptures, such as the Agnihotra and others.
But how is it understood that by the former [verse] the steadfastness in knowledge is taught for the renunciant, while by the second, steadfastness in action is taught for one incapable of that?
It is said: do you not remember what was stated regarding the immovable contradiction between knowledge and action, as firm as a mountain?

In this context as well, it has been stated: "He who desires to live should perform action," "All this is enveloped by the Lord," "By that which is renounced, you should enjoy," and "Do not covet the wealth of anyone.
Furthermore, from the injunction for renunciation (saṃnyāsa): "One should not covet either life or death; one should go to the forest, and from there, one should not return again."
And he will describe the difference in the fruits of both.
These two alone are the paths that have emerged most clearly: the path of action (kriyā-patha) in the former [stage] and renunciation (saṃnyāsa) in the latter.
Through the path of cessation (nivṛtti-mārga), there is the relinquishing of the threefold desire.
Of these two, the path of renunciation alone excels;
as it is said in the Taittirīyaka: "Renunciation alone excelled.
And: "There are these two paths upon which the Vedas are established..."
The dharma characterized by worldly involvement has been understood, as has that which is characterized by cessation.”
Having reflected thus upon his son, the venerable Vyāsa, the teacher of the Vedas, spoke this with certainty; and we shall demonstrate the distinction between these two.

Now, this mantra is commenced for the purpose of censuring the ignorant: "Those worlds called asurya, shrouded in blind darkness—to those they go after death, whoever among men are slayers of the Self. (Īśa Upaniṣad 3)
In relation to the non-dual state of the Supreme Self, even gods and others are "asuras" (non-gods), and the worlds belonging to them are called "asurya.
The word *nāma* is an indeclinable particle used without specific meaning.
Those worlds are the fruits of karma.
Births (*janmāni*) are so called because they are perceived, seen, and experienced.

Enveloped—that is, covered—by blindness, which is ignorance consisting of non-perception, namely *tamas*, they go after death, having abandoned this body, to those [births] ending with the immobile [beings], according to their karma and according to their learning.
They are "slayers of the self" (*ātmahan*) because they destroy the self.
Who are those people who are ignorant?
How do they constantly harm themselves?

Because of the defect of ignorance, they disregard the existing Self; and thus they neglect the function and fruit of the existing Self, which is characterized by the realization of such states as freedom from old age and death.

Because it has become concealed as if destroyed by that [ignorance], ordinary ignorant people are called "slayers of the self" (ātmahan). Indeed, through that fault of slaying the self, they wander in saṃsāra. (Īśopaniṣad Bhāṣya 3)

By the destruction of that Self, the ignorant transmigrate; by the opposite of that, wise people are liberated and are not destroyers of the Self. What is the true nature of that Self? It is said: It is motionless, one, swifter than the mind; the gods did not overtake it as it sped on before them.
While standing still, it outstrips others who run; in it Mātariśvan places the waters. (Īśa Upaniṣad 4)

"Unwavering" means not wavering; the root *ejṛ* signifies trembling, and trembling is movement, which is the falling away from one's own state. Thus, the meaning is that it is always of a single uniform nature, being devoid of that [movement].
And that [Self] is one in all beings, swifter than the mind—that is, more rapid than the mind characterized by volition and the like.
How can it be said to be contradictory to call this "swifter than the mind" and also "fixed" (dhruva), meaning immovable?
This is not a fault.

Because it is possible [to describe it] both as being without attributes (*nirupādhi*) and as possessing attributes (*upādhimat*), it is here described by its own unconditioned nature as "the one that does not move. Since it follows the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the mind—the internal organ characterized by resolve and doubt—it is well known in the world that the mind is the swiftest; for the mind, while residing in the body, reaches distant places such as the world of Brahmā through its volition in a mere instant. Thus, the swiftness of the mind is established in common experience.

When that mind travels swiftly to the world of Brahmā and other realms, the manifestation of the Self's consciousness is perceived as if it had already arrived; therefore, [the text] says it is "swifter than the mind. The gods—the senses such as sight and the rest—do not reach this aforementioned reality of the Self; they have not attained it.
The mind is swifter than those [senses]; because it is separated by the operations of the mind, even the mere appearance of the Self does not become an object for the gods.
Because it moves even before the swift mind, having already gone everywhere due to its all-pervasiveness like space—
that reality of the Self (ātmatattva), which is devoid of all the attributes of transmigratory existence— is indeed changeless in its own unconditioned nature; yet,
appearing as if manifold to the ignorant and deluded, it experiences all the transformations of transmigratory existence produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
It is said that [the Self] appears as distinct for every body.
As it runs—that is, as it moves swiftly—it surpasses others who are different from itself, such as the mind, speech, and the sense organs; it goes as if having surpassed them.
He himself shows the meaning of "as if" by saying "standing," which means being itself devoid of modification.

When that reality of the Self exists as the Mother-Wind (mātariśvan), whose nature is eternal consciousness— the wind which is the vital breath of all living beings, consisting of activity, upon which the collection of effects and instruments depends, which is woven across and through it, and which is known as the "Thread" (sūtra) that sustains the entire universe— that is the Mother-Wind.

The meaning is that he bestows—that is, distributes—the *apah* (actions), characterized by the movements of living beings, as well as those characterized by the flaming, burning, illuminating, raining, and so forth of fire, the sun, rain-clouds, and the like;
or alternatively, he sustains them, as in: “From fear of him the wind blows” (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8).
This is because of such scriptural passages as these.
The meaning is that all modifications, such as those of the body and the organs, occur only while the eternally conscious nature of the Self—which is the substratum of everything—exists.
There is no redundancy in the mantras; thus he speaks again of the meaning already stated in the previous mantra:
"It moves, and it moves not; it is far, and it is near;
it is within all this, and it is outside of all this. (Īśa Upaniṣad 5)
That very reality of the Self which has been introduced under discussion—that moves and that same thing does not move; meaning that while it is inherently unmoving, it appears as if moving.
Furthermore, it is "far," as if distant, because it is unattainable by the ignorant even in hundreds of millions of years.
The phrase *tad u antike* is to be analyzed as follows: it is "in the vicinity" (*antike*) or near; because it is the very Self (*ātmatva*) of the wise, it is not only far away but also near.
It is within that—that is, inside this entire universe—as it is said: "He who is the Self within all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4).

1) According to this scriptural statement, because it pervades the exterior of all this world—which consists of name, form, and action—it is like space; and because it is of unsurpassed subtlety, it is within.
Furthermore, according to the teaching that "it is indeed a mass of consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13), it is also without interval.
But he who perceives all beings in the Self alone, and the Self in all beings, does not shrink away from them. (Isa Upaniṣad 6)

The meaning is that the wandering mendicant who seeks liberation perceives all beings— from the unmanifest (*avyakta*) down to the stationary— within the Self alone, and does not perceive them as distinct from the Self;

and he perceives the Self within all those very beings, regarding it as their own Self, just as "I" am the Self of this body, which is a composite of causes and effects— the witness of all cognitions, the conscious one, absolute and devoid of qualities.

"By this very nature, I alone am the Self of all beings from the unmanifest down to the stationary; he who perceives the Self as undifferentiated within all beings does not, on account of that very perception, feel loathing—that is, he does not feel disgust.
This is a restatement of what has already been established."
For indeed, disgust arises for one who perceives anything other than the Self as defiled;
but for one who perceives only the Self as absolutely pure and without interruption, there is no separate object that could serve as a cause for disgust—this is self-evident.
Therefore, he does not feel loathing. (IsUpBh_6)
Another mantra also expresses this very same meaning:
"When for the one who knows all beings have become the Self alone, what delusion and what sorrow can there be for him who perceives that oneness? (Īśa Upaniṣad 7)

At whatever time, through the vision of the ultimate Self, all those very elements have become the Self alone— or rather, for one who knows the ultimate reality, the Self alone remains concealed as that reality— at that time, and within that Self, what delusion could there be, and what sorrow?
For sorrow and delusion arise from the lack of knowledge regarding the seeds of desire and action.

But for one who perceives the pure oneness of the Self, which is like the sky, [the question arises]: "What delusion, what sorrow? By thus implying that sorrow and delusion—the effects of ignorance—are impossible, it is demonstrated that transmigratory existence, along with its cause, is absolutely severed.
Regarding the nature of this Self that has been described by the preceding mantras, this mantra declares what its characteristic is in its own form:
"He has pervaded all—pure, bodiless, woundless, without sinews, clean, unpierced by evil.
He is the seer, the wise one, the all-pervading, the self-existent; he has established the objects according to their true nature for eternal years. (Īśa Upaniṣad 8)
That aforementioned Self has pervaded—meaning it has gone everywhere, surrounding all things, being all-pervasive like space;
it is pure (*śukram*), meaning luminous and radiant;
it is bodiless (*akāyam*), meaning devoid of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*).
"Without wound" means unscarred.
"Without sinews" means that in which sinews—that is, vessels—do not exist; thus it is "without sinews.
By these two terms, "without wound" and "without sinews," the gross body is negated.
"Pure" means stainless, devoid of the impurity of ignorance; this is a negation of the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*). "Unstruck by evil" means free from the evils of merit, demerit, and so forth.
Words such as "the bright" (*śukram*) and others should be understood by changing them into the masculine gender.
This is because the passage begins with "He has pervaded" (*sa paryagāt*) and concludes with masculine gender terms such as "the seer" (*kaviḥ*) and "the wise one" (*manīṣī*);
for "the seer" (*kaviḥ*) is one who has transcendent vision, the all-seeing.
As it is said: "There is no other seer than this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8).
This is because of such scriptural passages as these.
"Maniṣī" means the mover of the mind; the meaning is the omniscient Lord. "Paribhūḥ" means he who exists above all, transcending everything.

He is self-existent (*svayambhū*) because he exists by himself alone. He is self-existent because everyone who exists above him, and whoever exists above them—all such beings—exist by themselves alone. He is the eternally liberated Lord (*īśvara*). "Yathātathya" means being exactly as it is, due to his omniscience; from that state of being exactly as it is, [he knows] the objects through the means of accomplishing the fruits of actions as they truly are.
He "ordained" (vyadadhāt)—that is, he assigned—the duties to be performed; the meaning is that he distributed them appropriately.
"To the eternal years" (śāśvatībhyaḥ samābhyaḥ) means to the Prajāpatis known as the years.

Here, by means of the first mantra, the steadfastness in knowledge (*jñāna-niṣṭhā*) through the renunciation of all desires is declared as the first meaning of the Veda: “All this is to be enveloped by the Lord... do not covet the wealth of anyone. For those who are ignorant and desire to live, since steadfastness in knowledge is impossible, steadfastness in action (*karman-niṣṭhā*) is declared: “Performing actions here alone... one should desire to live. Furthermore, the distinction between these two types of steadfastness, as shown in the mantra, is also demonstrated in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*: “He desired: ‘May I have a wife’” (Bṛ. U. 1.4.17).
By such statements as these, it is established that the actions belong to the ignorant person who possesses desire.

From scriptural declarations such as, "The mind alone is his self, speech is his wife" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.17), it is understood with certainty that both ignorance and the state of possessing desire belong to one who is devoted to ritual action.

And thus, the fruit of that [knowledge] is the sevenfold creation of food and the abiding in the nature of the Self as the very self within those [beings]. Furthermore, by means of the renunciation of the three desires beginning with progeny, for those who know the Self, the state of abiding in the nature of the Self alone is shown—being contrary to devotion to ritual action—in such passages as: "What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self is this world? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).

However, for those renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*) who are established in knowledge, the true nature of the Self has been taught by means of the censure of the ignorant through the mantras beginning with "Those [who are ignorant] are called asuric" and ending with "He pervaded all that. For they alone are qualified here, not those possessed of desire.

And so it is said in the *Mantropaniṣad* of the Śvetāśvataras: "To those who have transcended the stages of life (*atyāśramin*), he fully proclaimed the supreme purifier, which is cherished by the assembly of sages" (Śve. U. 6.22).
21) Thus it has been explained in detail.
But for those performers of action who are devoted to action and desire to live while performing action, this is said:
"Into blinding darkness enter those who worship ignorance."
But for those who take delight in ignorance, it is as if they enter into deeper darkness.

But how is it understood that this applies [only] to some and not to all? It is said: Regarding the knowledge of the oneness of the Self which has been declared for one who is free from desire—by means of the sublation of the distinction between the goal and its means in the verse, "When, for the wise man, all beings have become the Self alone, then what delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives that oneness?"—no one who is undeluded would desire to combine that with any ritual action or any other form of knowledge.
In this context, however, a censure of the ignorant and others is made with the intention of collecting [the various means].

And therein, that which can logically or scripturally be combined with another is stated here; namely, that "wealth consisting of destiny" refers to knowledge concerning the deities presented in connection with ritual action, and not the knowledge of the Supreme Self.

Because of the hearing of separate fruits [for each], namely, "By knowledge, the world of the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.16), the censure of the performance of either one of those two—knowledge or action—is intended for the purpose of desiring their combination; it is not merely for the sake of censure, since a separate fruit is heard for each: "By knowledge they ascend there" and "By knowledge, the world of the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.16).
16) "No sacrificial offerings reach there" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.16), and "The world of the ancestors [is attained] by action.
Indeed, nothing prescribed by the scriptures can become something that ought not to be performed.
In that state, they enter blind darkness—darkness characterized by a lack of vision.

Who? Those who worship—that is, are devoted to and perform—only that ignorance characterized by the Agnihotra and other such rites; for "ignorance" here means action, since action is opposed to knowledge. This is the intended meaning.
Then, from that darkness consisting of ignorance, they enter into a darkness even greater—that is, much more intense—who are they?
Those who, having performed ritual action (*karman*), are devoted—meaning deeply attached—to knowledge alone, that is, to the knowledge of the deity.
Regarding this, he states the distinction between the intermediate results of knowledge and action as the reason for their being combined:
Otherwise, when two things—one possessing a fruit and one lacking a fruit—are in proximity, they would stand in the relationship of subordinate and principal; this is the meaning.
"Something quite different they say is attained through knowledge, and something else they say is attained through ignorance"—thus have we heard from the wise who explained this to us. (IsU 10)

They say that the fruit produced by knowledge is indeed distinct and separate; they declare this based on the Vedic revelation (Śruti): "By knowledge, the world of the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.16), and "By action, the world of the ancestors is made" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.16). Thus have we heard—the words of the wise and the learned.
The meaning is that this tradition (āgama) has come down through succession from those teachers who have explained—that is, expounded—to us both that action and that knowledge.
He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together—
having crossed over death by means of ignorance, he enjoys immortality through knowledge.
Since this is so, "knowledge and ignorance" means divine knowledge and ritual action;

for one who knows that both of these are to be performed together by a single person, it is said that for such a practitioner of combined practice, there is a connection with the goal of human life achieved through successive stages.

By means of "ignorance"—that is, ritual action such as the *agnihotra*—one crosses over death, which refers to natural activity and also to knowledge, both being denoted by the word "death"; having transcended both, one attains immortality through "knowledge," that is, through divine knowledge, which is the state of identity with the divine Self.
He attains it; for that which consists in going to the self of the deity is called the immortal.

Now, with the desire to enjoin the combined practice of the meditation on the Manifested (vyākṛta) and the Unmanifested (avyākṛta), a censure of each is stated individually: "Into blinding darkness enter those who worship the Unmanifested; into a darkness even greater than that enter those who delight in the Manifested. (Īśa Upaniṣad 12)

"Into blind darkness enter those who worship non-origination. Non-origination (*asambhūti*) is that which is other than origination (*sambhūti*). Origination is the manifestation of an effect; non-origination is its opposite, the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the cause known as ignorance (*avidyā*), called the "undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*).

Those who worship this non-origination—the undifferentiated primordial nature, the cause known as ignorance, which consists of the seeds of desire and action and whose essence is non-perception—enter into corresponding blind darkness.
They enter into darkness, which consists of non-perception;
from that, they enter as it were even more into a greater darkness—those who are devoted to *sambhūti*, that is, to the effected Brahman known as Hiraṇyagarbha.
Now he states the reason for the combination of both modes of worship, namely the difference in their constituent results:
"They say one thing on account of possibility; they say another on account of impossibility. Thus we have heard from the wise who explained it to us. (Īśa Upaniṣad 13)

The meaning is that they have explained the fruit resulting from the meditation on the *kāryabrahman* (the manifested Brahman) to be something entirely different and distinct—namely, the sovereignty characterized by powers such as *aṇimā* arising from *sambhava* or manifestation.
Likewise, they say that another result arises from *asambhava* or non-manifestation—that is, from the meditation on the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*).
As it has been said: "They enter into blind darkness," and what is called by the followers of the Purāṇas "merging into primordial nature" (*prakṛtilaya*)—thus we have heard.
"Those who explained to us the words of the wise" means those who have expounded the fruits of the meditations on the manifest (vyākṛta) and the unmanifest (avyākṛta).
Since this is so, the combination of the meditations on manifestation (*sambhūti*) and non-manifestation (*asambhūti*) is indeed appropriate, because they share a single human goal. Thus he says:
"He who knows both manifestation and destruction together—having crossed over death by means of destruction, he attains immortality through manifestation. (ĪśU 14)

He who knows both manifestation (*sambhūti*) and destruction (*vināśa*) together—wherein destruction is said to be non-different from its substrate, the effect, by virtue of being its inherent nature (*dharma*)—having crossed over death, which consists of the collection of defects such as lack of sovereignty, unrighteousness, and desire, through that meditation on it; for the fruit of meditating on Hiraṇyagarbha is the attainment of powers such as atomization (*aṇimā*).

Having thus transcended death in the form of lack of sovereignty and so forth, he attains immortality, characterized by dissolution into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*), through non-manifestation (*asambhūti*), which is the meditation on the unevolved (*avyākṛta*).

In the phrase "both origination and destruction," the elision of the vowel *a* (sandhi) should be understood here, in accordance with the scriptural teaching regarding the fruit of merging into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*).
The fruit achievable through human and divine means, characterized by the scriptures, extends up to the dissolution into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*).
This much is the course of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).

Beyond this, as previously stated, "for the one who knows, the Self alone becomes [all]"—this state of being the Self of all is the fruit of the steadfastness in knowledge resulting from the renunciation of all desires.
Thus, the two-fold meaning of the Veda—characterized by engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*)—has been elucidated here.

Regarding that, for the complete elucidation of the Vedic meaning characterized by engagement, which consists of injunctions and prohibitions, the *Brāhmaṇa* up to the end of the *Pravargya* section is employed; for the elucidation of the Vedic meaning characterized by withdrawal, the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* from that point onward is employed.

In this regard, one who desires to live performing the rites beginning with conception and ending with the funeral pyre, together with the knowledge concerning the lower Brahman, has it said: "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together—having crossed over death by means of ignorance, he enjoys immortality through knowledge.
It is now stated by which path he attains that immortality.
That which is the Truth is that Āditya who is this person within this orb, and also this person in the right eye; both of these are the Truth.

He who meditates upon Brahman and performs the prescribed actions, when the time of death arrives, petitions the Self whose essence is Truth for the door to its attainment, saying: "With a golden vessel...
[The verse continues: "With a golden vessel, the face of the Truth is covered."
Therefore, O Pūṣan, open it for me, who am devoted to the true Dharma, so that I may see.
"Golden" means as if made of gold; that is to say, consisting of light.
With that [disk] as a vessel serving as a cover, the mouth—the door—of the Truth residing in the solar orb is covered and concealed even from the Brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, O Pūṣan, uncover it, remove [the cover], for I am one whose truth is dharma through the meditation upon the Truth. I am he.

Or rather, [the word "satya"] means one whose nature is truth, for me; or else, it refers to the realization of your true self, who perceives the dharma as it actually is and practices that dharma accordingly.
O Pūṣan, sole seer, Yama, Sūrya, son of Prajāpati! Spread out your rays and gather together your splendor.
That form of yours which is most beautiful, that I behold. He who is yonder Person, that am I. (IsUp 16)

O Pūṣan! Because you nourish the world, you are Pūṣan; likewise, because you alone move as a solitary seer (*ekarṣi*), you are Ekarṣi—O Ekarṣi! Likewise, because you restrain everything, you are Yama—O Yama! Likewise, because you take up the rays, the vital breaths, and the essences, you are Sūrya—O Sūrya!
"O son of Prajāpati (prājāpatya)— he who is the offspring of Prajāpati!—
withdraw your rays;
gather them together, draw back that scorching light."

I behold that form of yours which is most auspicious and supremely beautiful, by virtue of the grace of your own self. Furthermore, I do not beg of you like a servant; rather, I seek that Person who resides within the solar orb, who is a constituent part of the sacred utterances (*vyāhṛti*), and who is called "Person" (*puruṣa*) because he has the form of a person, or because the entire world is filled by him through his nature as vital breath and intellect, or because he dwells within the city (*puri*) of the body.
I am that Person; I exist as such.
The wind has departed as the immortal breath; this body ends in ashes. Om! O Kratu, remember; remember what was done. O Kratu, remember; remember what was done. (IsUp 17)

Now, as I am about to die, let my vital breath (*prāṇa*), having abandoned its internal limitation (*adhyātma-pariccheda*), attain the immortal wind (*anila*) which is the cosmic self (*adhidaivata-ātmā*), the all-pervading *sūtrātmā*— this is the completion of the sentence. Furthermore, it should be understood that this subtle body (*liṅga*), refined by knowledge and action, shall depart,
because of the power inherent in the request for the path.
Now, let this body, when offered into the fire, become nothing but ashes.

"Om"—thus, because it has the nature of the *oṃ* syllable as its symbol (*pratīka*), the Brahman named Agni, whose essence is Truth, is spoken of non-differently [from that syllable]. O *kratu*, whose essence is volition!
"Remember that which is to be remembered by me; this time has now arrived, therefore remember it.

O Agni, remember all that has been cultivated and performed by me during this entire time—remember that action which was practiced by me from childhood onwards. O Kratu, remember! Remember what was done!"—the repetition "remember... remember" is for the sake of emphasis.
Again, he asks for the path with another mantra:
"O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O God who knows all ways;
remove from us the sin that leads astray; we shall offer you the most abundant word of homage. (Īśa Upaniṣad 18)
"O Agni, lead—cause me to go—by a *supathā*, a beautiful path.
The qualification *supathā* is intended to exclude the southern path.
I am weary of the southern path, characterized by coming and going; therefore, I entreat you: lead me by a beautiful path, free from repeated going and returning."

"For wealth" means for the enjoyment of the fruits of action; O God, you who know— that is, you who are aware of— all (viśvāni) deeds (vayunāni) or insights, [protect] us who are distinguished by the fruits of the aforementioned dharma.
Furthermore, "separate"—that is, disjoin and destroy—from us that crooked, deceitful sin (*enas*).
Then, being purified, we shall attain what is desired; this is the intention.
However, at present, we are not able to perform service for you.
We offer to you the most abundant expression of homage; that is to say, we shall serve you with salutations. As it is said:

"Having crossed over death through ignorance, one attains immortality through knowledge" (Īśa Upaniṣad 11); and "Having crossed over death through dissolution, one attains immortality through non-becoming" (Īśa Upaniṣad 14).
Having heard this, some harbor doubts;
therefore, for the purpose of dispelling them, we shall provide a brief investigation.
In that regard, first it is stated what the cause of the doubt is.
Why is it that by the word "knowledge" (vidyā) the primary knowledge of the Supreme Self alone is not understood, as well as immortality?
It is because the combination [of knowledge and action] is untenable due to the contradiction between unspoken knowledge of the Supreme Self and ritual action.
True.
However, no contradiction is perceived between contradiction and non-contradiction, because both are established by the authority of the scriptures (*śāstra*).
Just as the practice of ignorance and the meditation on knowledge are both established by the authority of the scriptures, so too are their respective contradictions and non-contradictions.

And just as it is understood from scripture that "one should not harm any living beings," yet this is subsequently sublated by scripture itself when it says "one should harm an animal in a sacrifice."

In the same way, this would apply to knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) as well, and there would be a combination of knowledge and action; for it is stated in scripture: "Far apart, contrary, and divergent are these two: ignorance and that which is knowledge" (KaU 1.2.4).
If it is argued that there is no contradiction because of the statement, "both knowledge and ignorance," we say no; for there is a contradiction in their causes, natures, and results.

If it is argued that there is indeed no contradiction because the injunction for their combination implies that the opposition between knowledge and ignorance is not absolute—since such an alternative [of opposition] is impossible—[we reply: no.
No; because their simultaneous occurrence is impossible.

If it is argued that knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) could exist sequentially within a single substratum, we say no; for when knowledge arises, ignorance has already been destroyed, and thus ignorance cannot exist within that same substratum.

For when the cognition arises that "fire is hot and luminous," it does not arise as the ignorance that "the fire is cold and non-luminous" in that very same substratum where that cognition has arisen; nor does it arise as doubt or as mere lack of knowledge. As it is said: "When for the one who knows all beings have become the Self alone, what delusion and what sorrow can there be for him who perceives that oneness? (Īśopaniṣad 7).

Thus, because of the scriptural statement regarding the impossibility of grief, delusion, and so forth, we have already explained that action— which has ignorance as its material cause— is likewise untenable. Furthermore,
the expression "he attains immortality" refers to a relative immortality.

If the word "knowledge" (vidyā) were taken to mean the knowledge of the Supreme Self (paramātman), then the request for the door, the path, and so forth—as expressed in the passage beginning with "with the golden one"—would be inappropriate.

Therefore, there is a combination [of means] through meditative worship (upāsanā), but not through the realization of the Supreme Self; thus, the meaning of the mantras is exactly as we have explained, and here the discussion is concluded.
Thus ends the commentary on the Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, the illustrious teacher and wandering mendicant of the supreme order.
